blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The English East India Company was established in 1600 by a royal charter of Queen Elizabeth I, evolving from a trading organization into a territorial power.
British dominance over French trading rivals was established through the three Carnatic Wars, ending French political ambitions with the Treaty of Paris (1763).
While the Battle of Plassey was won through conspiracy, the Battle of Buxar provided a decisive military victory over combined Indian forces.
The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) granted the Company Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, securing immense revenue control.
The Dual Government system introduced by Robert Clive split Diwani (revenue) and Nizamat (administration), causing severe economic exploitation.

blocks.content: British expansion in India was not a sudden event but a long, calculated process through which the English East India Company transformed itself from a trading organisation into a territorial power. This expansion was achieved mainly through wars, diplomacy, alliances, and exploitation of Indian political weakness. Understanding the wars fought by the British is crucial because military victories laid the foundation of colonial rule.

The English East India Company was established in 1600 by a royal charter of Queen Elizabeth I. Initially, it focused purely on trade, but declining Mughal authority, rivalry with European powers, and internal conflicts among Indian states provided the Company an opportunity to intervene politically.

The British and the French emerged as the two strongest European trading powers in India. Their rivalry was a part of the larger Anglo-French conflict in Europe and was reflected in India through the Carnatic Wars.

The First Carnatic War began as a result of the War of Austrian Succession in Europe. The French captured Madras, while the British retaliated by attacking French possessions. The war ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748), by which Madras was returned to the British. Though inconclusive, the war revealed the military weakness of Indian rulers.

The Second Carnatic War was fought over succession disputes in Hyderabad and Carnatic. The British supported Muhammad Ali, while the French backed Chanda Sahib. Robert Clive’s success at the Battle of Arcot (1751) proved decisive. The war ended with the Treaty of Pondicherry, establishing British superiority.

The Third Carnatic War coincided with the Seven Years’ War in Europe. The British decisively defeated the French, especially at the Battle of Wandiwash (1760). The Treaty of Paris (1763) ended French political ambitions in India, leaving Britain supreme.

The Battle of Plassey was fought between the British East India Company and Siraj-ud- Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal. The battle was won not through military strength but through conspiracy. Mir Jafar, commander of the Nawab’s army, betrayed Siraj-ud-Daulah. British victory gave them control over Bengal’s immense resources, marking the beginning of British political rule in India.
British expansion in India was primarily a military conquest supported by diplomacy and economic exploitation.
The Battle of Buxar was fought between the British and a combined force of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Bengal; Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh; and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam
II. The British victory was decisive and far more significant than Plassey. It resulted in the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), granting the Company Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

Introduced by Robert Clive in 1765, the Dual Government system divided authority between the Company and the Nawab. The Company collected revenue (Diwani) while the Nawab retained administrative responsibility (Nizamat). This system led to administrative chaos, corruption, and severe exploitation of peasants.
Mysore under Haider Ali and Tipu Sultan was the most formidable Indian power resisting British expansion.
Haider Ali defeated the British and forced them to sign the Treaty of Madras, restoring territories to pre-war positions.

rows: Combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula (Awadh), and Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor)
Won through conspiracy and the betrayal of Mir Jafar
Decisive military victory demonstrating superior military power
Gave the British control over Bengal's immense economic resources
Led to the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) and the grant of Diwani rights

blocks.content: Tipu Sultan inflicted severe defeats on the British. The war ended with the Treaty of Mangalore, recognising Tipu as a powerful ruler.
The British formed alliances with the Marathas and the Nizam. Tipu was defeated and forced to cede territory and pay heavy indemnity.
Tipu Sultan died defending Seringapatam. This marked the end of Mysore as an independent power.
The Marathas were the strongest Indian power after the decline of the Mughals.
The war ended with the Treaty of Salbai, recognising Madhavrao II as Peshwa.
British defeated Scindias and Bhonsles, establishing dominance in central India.
The Maratha Confederacy was completely crushed, making the British supreme power in India.

items: The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) in the Third Carnatic War definitively ended French colonial ambitions in India.
The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) granted Diwani rights (revenue collection) over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa to the British East India Company.
Under Robert Clive's Dual Government system (1765), the Company controlled Diwani while the Nawab held Nizamat (administrative responsibility).
Tipu Sultan died defending Seringapatam, which marked the complete collapse of Mysore as an independent power.

blocks.content: After the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, internal conflicts weakened the Sikh Empire.
British victory led to loss of Sikh territory and British influence in Punjab.
Punjab was annexed after British victory.
The British used wars, alliances, treaties, Subsidiary Alliance, and Doctrine of Lapse to expand their control.
British expansion in India was primarily a military conquest supported by diplomacy and economic exploitation. Wars destroyed Indian resistance and enabled the Company to establish colonial rule.
